lead: The simple Rankine cycle has two weak points. High boiler pressure raises the efficiency but makes the turbine exhaust too wet, and the cold feedwater takes in much of its heat at low temperature. Reheat fixes the first: the steam expands part-way, goes back to the boiler to be heated again, and then finishes its expansion, so the exhaust is drier. Regeneration fixes the second: a little steam is bled from the turbine to warm the feedwater, so the boiler adds heat at a higher mean temperature. Nearly every large steam plant uses both. This chapter works one example of each with the same steam conditions so the gains can be compared.
prereq: You need the simple cycle, its state numbering and the worked example of Rankine cycle and effect of pressure and temperature.

blocks.text: In the reheat cycle the states are: 1 high-pressure (HP) turbine inlet, 2 HP turbine exit, 3 reheater exit (low-pressure turbine inlet), 4 LP turbine exit, 5 condenser exit, 6 pump exit. Steam expands isentropically 1→2 to the reheat pressure, is reheated at constant pressure 2→3, usually back to about the initial steam temperature, and expands isentropically 3→4 to the condenser pressure.

items: w<sub>T</sub> = (h₁ − h₂) + (h₃ − h₄); w<sub>P</sub> = h₆ − h₅ = v<sub>f</sub>(p₁ − p₅);
q<sub>in</sub> = (h₁ − h₆) + (h₃ − h₂), the boiler plus the reheater;

blocks.text: The main gain is dryness: the LP expansion starts at a higher entropy, so the exhaust lies further right. The net work per kg also rises, which lowers the steam rate. The efficiency gain is small and depends on the reheat pressure; a reheat pressure of about a fifth to a quarter of the boiler pressure is a common choice. In current plants the reheat temperature is set equal to or close to the main steam temperature, about 540 to 600 °C.

sections.h3: Regenerative cycle with an open feedwater heater

blocks.text: In the regenerative cycle a fraction m of each kg of steam is bled from the turbine and mixed with the feedwater in an open feedwater heater, a mixing chamber at the bleed pressure. The states are: 1 turbine inlet, 2 bleed point, 3 turbine exit, 4 condenser exit, 5 exit of pump 1 (raised to heater pressure), 6 heater exit (saturated liquid at the bleed pressure), 7 exit of pump 2 (raised to boiler pressure). An open heater works at its own pressure, so each open heater needs a pump after it.

items: Heater energy balance (1 kg leaves as saturated liquid): m h₂ + (1 − m) h₅ = h₆, so m = (h₆ − h₅)/(h₂ − h₅).
Turbine work: w<sub>T</sub> = (h₁ − h₂) + (1 − m)(h₂ − h₃); only 1 − m kg expands to the condenser.
Pump work: w<sub>P</sub> = (1 − m)(h₅ − h₄) + (h₇ − h₆).
Heat added: q<sub>in</sub> = h₁ − h₇. Heat rejected: q<sub>out</sub> = (1 − m)(h₃ − h₄).

blocks.text: The boiler now receives water at about the saturation temperature of the bleed pressure instead of the condenser temperature. Heat that the simple cycle added at low temperature is now supplied by bled steam inside the cycle, so the mean temperature of heat addition rises. The net work per kg falls a little, because the bled steam does not finish its expansion. For one heater, a good bleed point is where the saturation temperature lies roughly halfway between the boiler and condenser saturation temperatures. With many heaters the cycle approaches the Carnot efficiency between the boiler and condenser temperatures (in kelvin).

A closed feedwater heater is a shell-and-tube exchanger: the feedwater passes through tubes and the bled steam condenses outside them, so the two streams do not mix and can be at different pressures. Its drain is either throttled back to a lower-pressure heater or the condenser, or pumped forward into the feed line. Plants use several closed heaters and one open heater that also removes dissolved gases (the deaerator).

examples.question: A steam plant takes steam at 60 bar and 500 °C. In a reheat cycle the steam expands to 10 bar, is reheated to 500 °C and expands to the condenser at 0.1 bar. Find the exhaust dryness, the net work, the heat added and the efficiency, and compare them with the simple cycle between 60 bar, 500 °C and 0.1 bar.
steps: State 1 (60 bar, 500 °C): h₁ = 3423.1 kJ/kg, s₁ = 6.8826 kJ/kg·K.
State 2: s₂ = 6.8826 is above s<sub>g</sub> = 6.585 at 10 bar, so the HP exhaust is superheated; interpolating in the 10 bar table gives h₂ = 2920.4 kJ/kg (about 240 °C).
State 3 (10 bar, 500 °C): h₃ = 3479.1 kJ/kg, s₃ = 7.7641 kJ/kg·K.
examples.answer: With reheat: exhaust dryness 0.949, w<sub>net</sub> = 1514.6 kJ/kg, q<sub>in</sub> = 3783.9 kJ/kg, η = 40.0%, steam rate 2.38 kg/kWh. Without: dryness 0.831, 1237.1 kJ/kg, η = 38.4%, 2.91 kg/kWh. Reheat mainly dries the exhaust and raises the work per kg.

examples.question: The same plant (60 bar, 500 °C, 0.1 bar, no reheat) bleeds steam at 5 bar to one open feedwater heater. The water leaves the heater as saturated liquid at 5 bar. Find the bled fraction, the net work, the heat added and the efficiency.
steps: State 2 (bleed, 5 bar, s = 6.8826): superheated (s<sub>g</sub> = 6.821 at 5 bar), h₂ = 2774.8 kJ/kg (about 163 °C). State 3 (0.1 bar): h₃ = 2180.0 kJ/kg, from the simple cycle.
State 6 (saturated liquid at 5 bar, 151.8 °C): h₆ = 640.09 kJ/kg, v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001093 m³/kg. Pump 2: 0.001093 × (6000 − 500) = 6.01 kJ/kg, so h₇ = 646.10 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: m = 0.173 kg per kg of steam; w<sub>net</sub> = 1133.6 kJ/kg; q<sub>in</sub> = 2777.0 kJ/kg; η = 40.8% against 38.4% for the simple cycle. The work per kg falls by 8%, but the heat added falls by 14%.

traps: In the reheat cycle the heat added includes the reheater, (h₃ − h₂). Leaving it out gives η = 1514.6/3225.2 = 47.0%, an impossible jump.
In the regenerative cycle only (1 − m) kg goes through the condenser and pump 1. Multiplying every term by 1 kg overstates the turbine work and the heat rejected.
An open heater needs a pump after it, because the heater is at the bleed pressure, not the boiler pressure. A sketch with one pump before the heater and none after it is wrong.
Check whether the steam at a bleed or reheat pressure is wet or superheated before choosing the table: compare s with s<sub>g</sub> at that pressure.
Reheat is for dryness and work; regeneration is for efficiency. Writing "reheat greatly raises efficiency" loses marks.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of reheating in a steam power plant?
quiz.a: To keep the turbine exhaust dry enough at high boiler pressure (less blade erosion) and to raise the net work per kg of steam; the efficiency gain is small.

quiz.q: Give one difference between an open and a closed feedwater heater.
quiz.a: An open heater mixes bled steam with feedwater at one pressure; a closed heater keeps them apart in a shell-and-tube exchanger, so they can be at different pressures.

quiz.q: Why does regeneration raise the cycle efficiency even though it lowers the work per kg?
quiz.a: The feedwater is warmed by bled steam inside the cycle, so the boiler no longer adds the low-temperature part of the heat. The mean temperature of heat addition rises, and the heat added falls more than the work does.

quiz.q: In an open heater, h₂ = 2800 kJ/kg, h₅ = 200 kJ/kg and h₆ = 700 kJ/kg. Find the bled fraction.
From the reheat example, find the steam flow for a 100 MW plant.
If the bleed pressure in the regenerative example is raised towards 60 bar or lowered towards 0.1 bar, what happens to the gain, and why?
quiz.a: The gain falls towards zero at both ends. Near 60 bar almost no steam is bled usefully and the heater barely warms the water; near 0.1 bar the heater warms the water by almost nothing. The best single bleed lies between, near the halfway saturation temperature.

quiz.q: The simple cycle at 60 bar, 500 °C has exhaust dryness 0.831. Which change, reheat or one open heater, would you choose to fix blade erosion, and what does the other change do instead?
quiz.a: Reheat: it raises the exhaust dryness to 0.949. One open heater leaves the exhaust dryness at 0.831 (the expansion line is the same) but raises η from 38.4% to 40.8%.

beyond: Large plants use double reheat and seven or eight feedwater heaters, with a deaerator as the one open heater. Plant designers optimise the bleed pressures and reheat pressure with cycle software, and supercritical units run without a boiling stage at all. Search for "feedwater heater train", "double reheat supercritical plant" and "heat balance diagram steam turbine".

(b) The regenerative example: 0.173 kg of each kg is bled at 5 bar into the open heater, and each pressure level has its own pump.
